title: Learning to Think Mathematically: Problem Solving, Metacognition and Sense-Making in Mathematics maths.com/resourcesnew/8.%20Research/Problem%20Solving/Learning%20to%20think%20mathema
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), October 24, 2024 — original paper: https://mrbarton
summary: This entry captures Barton's summary of Alan Schoenfeld's seminal paper on what it means to think mathematically and how classrooms can cultivate it. Schoenfeld argues that mathematical thinking is fundamentally a social process, not simply the accumulation of facts and procedures — it requires developing a mathematical point of view, tolerance for uncertainty, and genuine valuing of sense-making and discovery. He proposes a framework of mathematical cognition spanning knowledge base, problem-solving strategies, monitoring and control (metacognition), beliefs and affects, and practices, and uses it to argue for a shift away from rote-memorization-heavy instruction toward inquiry- and problem-solving-based teaching. A recurring warning is that students' beliefs about mathematics are shaped by what they're consistently asked to do: if every problem can be solved in a few minutes, students conclude — wrongly — that all real maths works that way, so teachers need to be deliberate about the kinds of problems and struggle they expose students to.
points: Mathematical thinking is framed as fundamentally social and dispositional — comfort with uncertainty and valuing sense-making — not just knowing facts and procedures.

Schoenfeld's five-part cognitive framework (knowledge base, strategies, metacognition, beliefs/affect, practices) gives teachers a structured way to diagnose what's missing when a student 'can't problem-solve.'
Students' beliefs about what mathematics is are shaped by classroom experience: constant exposure to quick, closed problems teaches students a false picture of what doing maths actually involves.
Assessment should be realigned to match instructional goals — assessing thinking and problem-solving (open questions, portfolios, observed collaboration), not just recall of facts and procedures.
quotes: This paper explores what it means to think mathematically and how this can be achieved in the classroom.

The author argues that learning to think mathematically is a social process that involves more than just memorizing facts and procedures; it requires developing a mathematical point of view, becoming comfortable with uncertainty, and valuing the processes of mathematical discovery and sense-making.

Students' beliefs about mathematics are shaped by their experiences in the classroom. If students are consistently given problems that can be solved in a few minutes or less, they will come to believe that all mathematics problems can be solved quickly, which is not the case.

Teachers who believe that mathematics is a fixed body of knowledge that must be memorized will likely create learning environments that are very different from those created by teachers who believe that mathematics is a dynamic and creative discipline.
If we want students to develop mathematical power, we need to assess them on their ability to think mathematically and solve problems, not just on their ability to memorize facts and procedures.
Problem-solving should be the focus of school mathematics, and it should be taught in a way that is authentic to the discipline.
